questions.question: A patient develops new hypertension at 30 weeks without proteinuria or other end-organ findings. Which classification is most appropriate initially?
choices: Gestational hypertension, with continued evaluation for evolving preeclampsia
Chronic hypertension by definition
Normal pregnancy physiology
Postpartum preeclampsia
questions.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or qualifying organ dysfunction is initially classified as gestational hypertension, but it can evolve and requires obstetric surveillance.

questions.question: Which statement about proteinuria and preeclampsia is most accurate?
choices: A negative urine dipstick permanently excludes preeclampsia
Proteinuria alone determines every delivery decision
Protein testing replaces symptom assessment
Proteinuria is not required when qualifying maternal organ dysfunction or severe features are present
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia may be diagnosed without proteinuria when defined end-organ findings are present. Urine testing must be integrated with symptoms, blood pressure, labs, gestational age, and fetal status.

questions.question: Which presentation requires immediate obstetric emergency evaluation?
choices: A request for nutrition counseling
Mild ankle swelling without other symptoms and normal evaluation
Severe blood pressure with persistent headache and visual change
A stable home pressure log within the established plan
questions.explanation: Severe hypertension with neurologic symptoms may represent preeclampsia with severe features and carries stroke and seizure risk. Emergency obstetric assessment is required.

questions.question: A patient with chronic hypertension develops new proteinuria and rising liver enzymes after 20 weeks. What should the FNP suspect?
choices: Isolated white-coat hypertension
Superimposed preeclampsia
Resolution of chronic hypertension
Normal hemodilution only
questions.explanation: New preeclamptic findings in a patient with chronic hypertension raise concern for superimposed preeclampsia and require prompt obstetric evaluation.

questions.question: Which patient is among those at high risk for whom current guidance supports consideration of low-dose aspirin prevention after 12 weeks?
choices: A patient with prior preeclampsia or chronic hypertension
Every pregnant patient regardless of history
Only patients with seasonal allergies
A patient who is already postpartum
questions.explanation: Prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, multifetal pregnancy, pregestational diabetes, kidney disease, and autoimmune disease are high-risk factors. Prevention should follow current guidance and the prenatal plan.

questions.question: Why can a normal initial laboratory panel fail to end the evaluation of a symptomatic patient?
choices: Laboratory tests are never useful
Only fetal testing matters
Symptoms cannot precede laboratory changes
Preeclampsia can evolve, and serial clinical assessment may be needed when symptoms or pressure remain concerning
questions.explanation: Pregnancy-related hypertensive disease is dynamic. Persistent or worsening symptoms require reassessment and appropriate obstetric disposition even if initial tests are reassuring.

questions.question: Ten days postpartum, a patient has severe headache, dyspnea, and facial swelling. What is the safest action?
choices: Schedule a routine annual physical
Recommend repeated home checks for several days before calling
Arrange emergency evaluation for postpartum hypertensive and cardiopulmonary complications
Reassure because delivery is complete
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia and other life-threatening complications can first present postpartum. Severe headache and dyspnea require immediate evaluation.

questions.question: What is the best approach to an unexpected high blood-pressure reading during pregnancy?
choices: Delay all action until the next prenatal month
Repeat with correct technique while simultaneously assessing symptoms and urgency
Ignore it if the patient feels well
Use an unvalidated wrist cuff as the final value
questions.explanation: Accurate technique matters, but confirmation must not delay escalation when symptoms, severe pressure, or instability indicate urgent disease.

questions.question: Which symptom cluster most strongly reflects possible hepatic involvement in preeclampsia?
choices: Right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain with abnormal liver studies
Isolated nasal congestion
Mild wrist discomfort after typing
Stable appetite with normal examination
questions.explanation: Severe epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain and elevated transaminases may reflect hepatic involvement and are high-risk preeclamptic findings.

questions.question: What longitudinal action remains important after a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia?
choices: Remove hypertension history after six weeks
Avoid discussing future pregnancy
Stop all medication without review
Transition to primary care for blood-pressure and long-term cardiovascular-risk follow-up
questions.explanation: Preeclampsia identifies increased future cardiovascular risk. Postpartum transition should include BP monitoring, medication review, primary-care follow-up, and future-pregnancy counseling.
